claim: Nrxn1 mRNA is found at higher levels in VTA DA neurons compared to SNc DA neurons (12,280±369 vs 10,698±359 FKPM, p<0.005).
source: We found that while mRNA for all three forms of Nrxn are found at high levels in both VTA and SNc DA neurons, Nrxn1 is found at higher levels in VTA neurons, Nrxn2 is similarly expressed in both populations and Nrxn3 is found at higher levels in SNc neurons (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data presented in Table 1 showing FKPM values and statistical comparison.

claim: Nrxn2 mRNA is similarly expressed in both VTA and SNc DA neurons (13,505±1042 vs 14,038±82 FKPM, p>0.05).
source: We found that while mRNA for all three forms of Nrxn are found at high levels in both VTA and SNc DA neurons, Nrxn1 is found at higher levels in VTA neurons, Nrxn2 is similarly expressed in both populations and Nrxn3 is found at higher levels in SNc neurons (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data presented in Table 1 showing FKPM values and statistical comparison.

claim: Nrxn3 mRNA is found at higher levels in SNc DA neurons compared to VTA DA neurons (12,857±239 vs 7854±295 FKPM, p<0.001).
source: We found that while mRNA for all three forms of Nrxn are found at high levels in both VTA and SNc DA neurons, Nrxn1 is found at higher levels in VTA neurons, Nrxn2 is similarly expressed in both populations and Nrxn3 is found at higher levels in SNc neurons (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data presented in Table 1 showing FKPM values and statistical comparison.

claim: Sox6 mRNA is found at higher levels in SNc DA neurons compared to VTA DA neurons (2862±63 vs 195±17 FKPM, p<0.001).
source: Validating the precision of VTA and SNc dissections, we found that mRNA of the transcription factor Sox6 was found at higher levels in SNc neurons, while that of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT2 and of the calcium binding protein calbindin-1 were found at higher levels in VTA neurons, in line with previous work (Table 1; Dal Bo et al., 2004; Panman et al., 2014; Pereira Luppi et al., 2021; Poulin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data in Table 1 and is consistent with previous literature cited.

claim: VGLUT2 (Slc17a6) mRNA is found at higher levels in VTA DA neurons compared to SNc DA neurons (1953±144 vs 587±34 FKPM, p<0.001).
source: Validating the precision of VTA and SNc dissections, we found that mRNA of the transcription factor Sox6 was found at higher levels in SNc neurons, while that of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT2 and of the calcium binding protein calbindin-1 were found at higher levels in VTA neurons, in line with previous work (Table 1; Dal Bo et al., 2004; Panman et al., 2014; Pereira Luppi et al., 2021; Poulin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data in Table 1 and is consistent with previous literature cited.

claim: Calbindin-1 (Calb1) mRNA is found at higher levels in VTA DA neurons compared to SNc DA neurons (8373±519 vs 1791±49 FKPM, p<0.001).
source: Validating the precision of VTA and SNc dissections, we found that mRNA of the transcription factor Sox6 was found at higher levels in SNc neurons, while that of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT2 and of the calcium binding protein calbindin-1 were found at higher levels in VTA neurons, in line with previous work (Table 1; Dal Bo et al., 2004; Panman et al., 2014; Pereira Luppi et al., 2021; Poulin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data in Table 1 and is consistent with previous literature cited.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO mice show no significant difference in latency to fall on the accelerating rotarod task compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (F(1, 14)=1.43, p=0.25).
source: The measure of latency to fall did not reveal a significant difference between the genotypes, with all groups showing a comparable increase in performance (Figure 1B, two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 14)=1.43, p=0.25).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the rotarod test.

claim: Both DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice show equivalent learning on the rotarod task when comparing first and last sessions (two-way ANOVA, main effect of training session, F(1, 28)=21.72, p<0.0001).
source: Similar results were obtained when evaluating the progression of the performance of the mice by comparing the first and last sessions, with mice of both genotypes showing equivalent learning (Figure 1C; two-way ANOVA, main effect of training session, F(1, 28)=21.72, p<0.0001; Sidak's multiple comparisons test, S1 vs S9: WT, p=0.022 and KO, p=0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing performance across sessions.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO mice show a tendency for impaired performance on a more challenging rotarod task (F(1, 16)=4.00, p=0.06).
source: In this cohort, the latency to fall was not significantly different in DAT::NrxnsKO compared to DAT::NrxnsWT, although a tendency for impaired performance was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1, 16)=4.00, p=0.06).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from a more challenging rotarod protocol.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO mice require significantly more time to climb down the pole compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (8.14±0.93 s vs 5.80±0.53 s, p=0.034).
source: In the pole test, no difference was observed between genotypes for the time required for the mice to orient downward (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E; unpaired t-test, p=0.15) but interestingly the time required to climb down the pole was significantly higher for the DAT::NrxnsKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; unpaired t-test, p=0.034).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from the pole test.

claim: Basal locomotion in the open field over 60 minutes is not different between DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice (F(1; 18)=3.77, p=0.068).
source: Basal locomotion in the open field over a 60 min period was also not different between genotypes (Figure 1E; two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1; 18)=3.77, p=0.068).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of locomotor activity data.

claim: Cocaine-induced locomotion (20 mg/kg) is comparable between DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice (F(1; 16)=0.64, p=0.43).
source: Although locomotion induced by cocaine (20 mg/kg) was comparable between genotypes (Figure 1F, two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1; 16)=0.64, p=0.43), locomotion induced in response to amphetamine (5 mg/kg) was strongly reduced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (Figure 1G, two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1; 13)=6.66, main effect of genotype, p=0.023).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of cocaine-induced locomotor activity data.

claim: Amphetamine-induced locomotion (5 mg/kg) is strongly reduced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (F(1; 13)=6.66, p=0.023).
source: Although locomotion induced by cocaine (20 mg/kg) was comparable between genotypes (Figure 1F, two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1; 16)=0.64, p=0.43), locomotion induced in response to amphetamine (5 mg/kg) was strongly reduced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (Figure 1G, two-way ANOVA, repeated measures, F(1; 13)=6.66, main effect of genotype, p=0.023).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of amphetamine-induced locomotor activity data.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice show similar preference for sucrose over water in a two-bottle choice test (two-way ANOVA, main effect of choice F(3; 20)=487.0; Tukey's multiple comparisons test, TD1, -2, -3, water versus sucrose, all genotypes, p<0.0001).
source: Similarly, during the next three testing days (TD1, -2, and -3), when mice were given a choice between water and sucrose, DAT::NrxnsKO and WT mice both showed a similar marked preference for the sucrose bottle (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H; two-way ANOVA, main effect of choice F(3; 20)=487.0; Tukey's multiple comparisons test, TD1, -2, -3, water versus sucrose, all genotypes, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of sucrose preference test data.

claim: TH surface area is unchanged in both vSTR and dSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice.
source: We found that TH surface area was unchanged in both the vSTR and dSTR (Figure 2A–B , and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: VMAT2 surface area is significantly increased in the vSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice (168.3±28.27% of control, p=0.045), but not in the dSTR.
source: However, the surface of VMAT2 immunoreactivity was significantly increased in the vSTR, but not in the dSTR, of the KO mice (Figure 2A–B , and G; vSTR, unpaired t-test, Welch's corrected, p=0.045).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: DAT surface area is significantly decreased in the vSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice (59.00±10.71% of control, p=0.034), but not in the dSTR.
source: In contrast, DAT surface area was significantly decreased in the vSTR, but not in the dSTR, of the KO mice (Figure 2C and F; vSTR, unpaired t-test, p=0.034).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TH, VMAT2, and DAT signal intensity are unchanged in both vSTR and dSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: In addition to the surface of immunopositive signal, the average intensity was also quantified. TH, VMAT2, and DAT signal intensity of DAT::NrxnsKO mice were unchanged in both vSTR and dSTR (Figure 2A–D, F, H and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TH-positive dopaminergic terminals in the vSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice are not different from DAT::NrxnsWT mice in terms of perimeter (p=0.94), length (p=0.94), width (p=0.43), or surface area (p=0.92).
source: Furthermore, TH-positive dopaminergic terminals in the vSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice were not different compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice in terms of their overall perimeters (P) (Figure 3C–D; unpaired t-test, p=0.94), length (L) (Figure 3E, unpaired t-test, p=0.94), width (w) (Figure 3F, unpaired t-test, p=0.43), or surface area (Figure 3G, unpaired t-test, p=0.92).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The synaptic incidence of TH-positive terminals is 6.34% in DAT::NrxnsKO mice and 4.95% in control mice.
source: The synaptic incidence of TH-positive terminals was 6.34% (12 terminals with a PSD domain/189 TH-positive varicosities) for DAT::NrxnsKO mice and 4.95% (5 terminals with a PSD domain/101 TH-positive varicosities) for control mice (data not shown), a low proportion in line with previous work (Bérubé-Carrière et al., 2012; Stuber et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy data and is consistent with previous literature cited.

claim: The size of the postsynaptic density (PSD) is similar between DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice (232.8±23.40 nm vs 197.1±35.71 nm, p=0.54).
source: Among these synaptic TH-positive varicosities, the size of the PSD was similar (Figure 3H, unpaired t-test, p=0.54).
evidence: The claim is supported by electron microscopy quantification data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Peak DA overflow is not different between DAT::NrxnsWT and DAT::NrxnsKO mice in normal extracellular saline in both vSTR and dSTR.
source: In the first series of experiments performed in normal extracellular saline, we found no difference in peak DAo between the DAT::NrxnsWT and DAT::NrxnsKO mice (Figure 4A–B and E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The tau value of DA recovery in the vSTR is significantly higher in DAT::NrxnsKO compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (0.42±0.02 vs 0.35±0.02, p=0.008).
source: However, an examination of the kinetics of DAo, often used to identify changes in DA release efficiency and reuptake (Yorgason et al., 2011), revealed that the tau value of DA recovery in the vSTR was significantly higher in DAT::NrxnsKO compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (Figure 4A and C, unpaired t-test, p=0.008).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4 and references a method from previous literature.

claim: The tau value of DA recovery in the dSTR is significantly higher in DAT::NrxnsKO compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (0.45±0.03 vs 0.36±0.02, p=0.019).
source: We also observed a similar increase in tau for the rate of DA recovery in the dSTR (Figure 4E and G; unpaired t-test, p=0.019).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Paired-pulse depression is significantly enhanced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT in the vSTR (p=0.04).
source: Interestingly, the level of paired-pulse depression was significantly enhanced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT in the vSTR (Figure 4D; unpaired t-test, p=0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Paired-pulse depression in the dSTR is similar in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT mice (p=0.62).
source: However, in the dSTR, paired-pulse depression was similar in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 4H; unpaired t-test, p=0.62).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Baclofen-induced inhibition of DA overflow is not different between DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice.
source: We found that baclofen-induced inhibition of DAo was not different across genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Peak DA release in the presence of DHβE is reduced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT in both vSTR (p=0.0502) and dSTR (p=0.03).
source: Strikingly, peak DA release was reduced in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT in both the vSTR and dSTR (vSTR, Mann-Whitney test, p=0.0502 and dSTR, Mann-Whitney test, p=0.03) (Figure 4I–J , and M–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data in the presence of nicotinic receptor antagonist shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rate of DA recovery in the presence of DHβE is unchanged between DAT::NrxnsKO and DAT::NrxnsWT mice.
source: The rate of DA recovery was unchanged (Figure 4K and O).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data in the presence of DHβE shown in Figure 4.

claim: Paired-pulse depression of direct DA release in the presence of DHβE is similar in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT mice in both vSTR (p=0.73) and dSTR (p=0.87).
source: Similarly, paired-pulse depression of this direct DA release was similar in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to WT mice (vSTR: unpaired t-test, 0.73 and dSTR: unpaired t-test, p=0.87) (Figure 4L and P and Figure 4—figure supplement 1M–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by fast-scan cyclic voltammetry data in the presence of DHβE shown in Figure 4.

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs in the vSTR show a significant increase in amplitude in DAT::NrxnsKO mice compared to DAT::NrxnsWT mice (p=0.0014).
source: We found a significant increase in the amplitude of optically evoked IPSCs (oIPSCs) in MSNs recorded in vSTR slices prepared from DAT::NrxnsKO mice (Figure 5C; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.0014).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The decay time constant (tau) of GABA-mediated oIPSCs in the vSTR is unchanged in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.06).
source: Closer analysis of the kinetics of GABA-mediated oIPSCs in the vSTR revealed that the decay time constant (tau) was unchanged (Figure 5D; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.06) in DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: oIPSC delay and rise time in the vSTR are unchanged in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.49 and p=0.78).
source: The oIPSC delay and rise time were also unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D; unpaired t-tests p=0.49 and p=0.78).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No statistically significant changes in oIPSC amplitude are observed in the dSTR of DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.36).
source: We observed no statistically significant changes in oIPSC amplitude in DAT::NrxnsKO mice in the dSTR (Figure 5E; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.36).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: oIPSC decay time constant in the dSTR is unchanged in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.63).
source: oIPSC decay time constant was also unchanged (Figure 5F; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.63), as were the oIPSC delay and rise time (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–F; unpaired t-tests p=0.85 and p=0.38).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No genotype differences in optically evoked EPSCs are detected in either vSTR (p=0.77) or dSTR (p=0.92).
source: We did not detect genotype differences in optically evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) (Figure 6A; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.77, Figure 6B; Mann-Whitney test, p=0.92), which were otherwise blocked by the ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists CNQX and AP5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A small decrease in collybistin mRNA is detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.021).
source: However, using qRT-PCR, we did not detect major changes in expression of these genes in micro-dissected vSTR or dSTR, except for a small decrease in collybistin and LRRTM3 mRNA in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (unpaired t-test, p=0.021 and p=0.014, respectively) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small decrease in LRRTM3 mRNA is detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (p=0.014).
source: However, using qRT-PCR, we did not detect major changes in expression of these genes in micro-dissected vSTR or dSTR, except for a small decrease in collybistin and LRRTM3 mRNA in DAT::NrxnsKO mice (unpaired t-test, p=0.021 and p=0.014, respectively) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: SNc DA neurons globally show larger GABA uptake compared to VTA DA neurons (two-way ANOVA, main effect of region, F(1, 76)=53.35, p<0.001).
source: Interestingly, SNc DA neurons globally showed a larger GABA uptake compared to VTA DA neurons (Figure 7E; two-way ANOVA, main effect of region, F(1, 76)=53.35, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by GABA uptake assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: A global increase of GABA uptake is observed in DAT::NrxnsKO DA neurons compared to DAT::NrxnsWT DA neurons (two-way ANOVA, main effect of genotype, F(1, 76)=6.25, p=0.014).
source: Furthermore, we observed a global increase of GABA uptake in DAT::NrxnsKO DA neurons compared to DAT::NrxnsWT DA neurons (two-way ANOVA, main effect of genotype, F(1, 76)=6.25, p=0.014).
evidence: The claim is supported by GABA uptake assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Midbrain dopamine neurons are key regulators of basal ganglia functions.
source: Midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons are key regulators of basal ganglia functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about DA neuron function presented in the abstract.

claim: The axonal domain of DA neurons is highly complex, with a large subset of non-synaptic release sites and a smaller subset of synaptic terminals.
source: The axonal domain of these neurons is highly complex, with a large subset of non-synaptic release sites and a smaller subset of synaptic terminals from which in addition to DA, glutamate or GABA are also released.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about DA neuron anatomy presented in the abstract.

claim: DA neurons can co-release glutamate or GABA from a subset of synaptic terminals.
source: The axonal domain of these neurons is highly complex, with a large subset of non-synaptic release sites and a smaller subset of synaptic terminals from which in addition to DA, glutamate or GABA are also released.
evidence: This is a statement about DA neuron neurotransmitter co-release presented in the abstract.

claim: An emerging literature suggests that neuroligins regulate both DA neuron connectivity and neurotransmission.
source: An emerging literature suggests that neuroligins, trans-synaptic cell adhesion molecules, regulate both DA neuron connectivity and neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a summary statement about neuroligin function in DA neurons presented in the abstract.

claim: The contribution of neurexins to DA neuron function is unexplored.
source: However, the contribution of their major interaction partners, neurexins (Nrxns), is unexplored.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Neurexins are major interaction partners of neuroligins.
source: However, the contribution of their major interaction partners, neurexins (Nrxns), is unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between neurexins and neuroligins.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO mice exhibit normal basic motor functions.
source: Mice with conditional deletion of all Nrxns in DA neurons (DAT::NrxnsKO) exhibited normal basic motor functions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of behavioral findings presented in the abstract.

claim: DAT::NrxnsKO mice show an impaired locomotor response to amphetamine.
source: However, they showed an impaired locomotor response to the psychostimulant amphetamine.
evidence: This is a summary statement of behavioral findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Decreased levels of membrane DAT are detected in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: In line with an alteration in DA neurotransmission, decreased levels of the membrane DA transporter (DAT) and increased levels of the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) were detected in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice, along with reduced activity-dependent DA release.
evidence: This is a summary statement of immunohistochemistry findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Increased levels of VMAT2 are detected in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: In line with an alteration in DA neurotransmission, decreased levels of the membrane DA transporter (DAT) and increased levels of the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) were detected in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice, along with reduced activity-dependent DA release.
evidence: This is a summary statement of immunohistochemistry findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Reduced activity-dependent DA release is observed in DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: In line with an alteration in DA neurotransmission, decreased levels of the membrane DA transporter (DAT) and increased levels of the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) were detected in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice, along with reduced activity-dependent DA release.
evidence: This is a summary statement of FSCV findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings reveal an increase of GABA co-release from DA neuron axons in the striatum of DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: Strikingly, electrophysiological recordings revealed an increase of GABA co-release from DA neuron axons in the striatum of these mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of electrophysiology findings presented in the abstract.

claim: Neurexins act as regulators of the functional connectivity of DA neurons.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Nrxns act as regulators of the functional connectivity of DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the abstract.

claim: DA neurons from the VTA and SNc project densely to the vSTR and dSTR, respectively.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) project densely to the ventral striatum (vSTR) and to the dorsal striatum (dSTR), respectively (Descarries et al., 1980; Matsuda et al., 2009) and are critical regulators of basal ganglia functions, motivation, and cognition (Schultz, 2007; Surmeier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about DA neuron anatomy supported by citations.

claim: DA neurons are critical regulators of basal ganglia functions, motivation, and cognition.
source: Dopamine (DA) neurons from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) project densely to the ventral striatum (vSTR) and to the dorsal striatum (dSTR), respectively (Descarries et al., 1980; Matsuda et al., 2009) and are critical regulators of basal ganglia functions, motivation, and cognition (Schultz, 2007; Surmeier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about DA neuron function supported by citations.

claim: The connectivity of the DA system is predominantly non-synaptic.
source: The connectivity of the DA system is predominantly non-synaptic (Descarries et al., 2008; Ducrot et al., 2021; Wildenberg et al., 2021), with a majority of DA-releasing terminals not located in close apposition to a postsynaptic domain (Caillé et al., 1996; Descarries et al., 2008; Descarries et al., 1996; Descarries and Mechawar, 2000; Ducrot et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about DA system connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claim: A majority of DA-releasing terminals are not located in close apposition to a postsynaptic domain.
source: The connectivity of the DA system is predominantly non-synaptic (Descarries et al., 2008; Ducrot et al., 2021; Wildenberg et al., 2021), with a majority of DA-releasing terminals not located in close apposition to a postsynaptic domain (Caillé et al., 1996; Descarries et al., 2008; Descarries et al., 1996; Descarries and Mechawar, 2000; Ducrot et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about DA terminal anatomy supported by multiple citations.

claim: A smaller synaptic subset of DA neuron terminals has the ability to co-release glutamate or GABA.
source: A smaller synaptic subset of DA neuron terminals has the ability to co-release glutamate or GABA (Dal Bo et al., 2004; Mendez et al., 2008; Stuber et al., 2010; Sulzer et al., 1998; Tritsch et al., 2016; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about DA neuron co-transmission supported by multiple citations.

claim: Little is presently known about the molecular mechanisms underlying the formation and regulation of the complex axonal arbor and release sites established by DA neurons.
source: Despite the functional importance of DA in the brain, little is presently known about the molecular mechanisms underlying the formation and regulation of the complex axonal arbor and release sites established by DA neurons.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Only a limited number of studies have explored the molecular mechanisms underlying DA release.
source: Only a limited number of studies have until now explored the molecular mechanisms underlying DA release (Banerjee et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2020; Delignat-Lavaud et al., 2021; Ducrot et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2018; Mendez et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2019, Delignat-Lavaud et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement summarizes the state of the literature with citations.

claim: A growing body of work suggests that neuroligins directly or indirectly regulate the connectivity of DA neurons.
source: Interestingly, a growing body of work suggests that the trans-synaptic cell adhesion neuroligins (NLs) directly or indirectly regulate the connectivity of DA neurons.
evidence: This statement summarizes the state of the literature on neuroligins.

claim: Impaired DA-mediated motor behaviors were reported in C. elegans lacking NL-1.
source: Impaired DA-mediated motor behaviors were reported in Caenorhabditis elegans lacking NL-1 (Izquierdo et al., 2013; Rodríguez-Ramos et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement reports findings from previous studies with citations.

claim: Downregulation of NL-2 in striatal neurons was suggested to reduce the frequency of contacts between DA neuron axons and the dendrites of striatal neurons.
source: Downregulation of NL-2 in striatal neurons was also suggested to reduce the frequency of contacts between DA neuron axons and the dendrites of striatal neurons (Uchigashima et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement reports findings from a previous study with citation.

claim: Mutations in NL-3 in mice lead to impaired synaptic inhibition onto striatal D1 DA receptor expressing neurons.
source: Mutations in NL-3 in mice lead to impaired synaptic inhibition onto striatal D1 DA receptor expressing neurons (Rothwell et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement reports findings from a previous study with citation.

claim: Both NL-1 and NL-2 are permissive for the formation of synapse-like contacts by DA neuron axons.
source: Finally, both NL-1 and NL-2 are permissive for the formation of synapse-like contacts by DA neuron axons (Ducrot et al., 2021; Uchigashima et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement reports findings from previous studies with citations.

claim: Neuroligins mediate some of their cellular and synaptic effects by interacting with neurexins.
source: Although NLs mediate some of their cellular and synaptic effects by interacting with neurexins (Nrxns) (Chen et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015), the role of this family of presynaptic cell adhesion molecules in DA neurons is presently unexplored.
evidence: This statement describes the relationship between neuroligins and neurexins with citations.

claim: Neurexins were initially identified as α-latrotoxin receptors.
source: Nrxns were initially identified as α-latrotoxin receptors (Ushkaryov et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement provides historical context about neurexin discovery with citation.

claim: In mammals, neurexins are expressed in two principal forms: longer α-Nrxns isoforms and shorter β-Nrxns isoforms.
source: In mammals, Nrxns are expressed in two principal forms: longer α-Nrxns isoforms and shorter β-Nrxns isoforms (Tabuchi and Südhof, 2002).
evidence: This statement describes neurexin isoforms with citation.

claim: Neurexin proteins on axon terminals interact with postsynaptic neuroligin proteins and regulate synapse formation and function.
source: The Nrxn proteins on axon terminals interact with postsynaptic NL proteins and have been shown to regulate synapse formation and function (Graf et al., 2004; Ichtchenko et al., 1995; Ko et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement describes neurexin function with citations.

claim: Neuroligins only bind to neurexins, whereas neurexins have large numbers of splice variants with differential binding affinities with multiple postsynaptic partners.
source: NLs only bind to Nrxns, whereas Nrxns have large numbers of splice variants with differential binding affinities with multiple postsynaptic partners.
evidence: This statement describes the binding specificity of neuroligins and neurexins.

claim: Neurexins regulate neurotransmission through different mechanisms in a cell type-specific manner.
source: Several key studies using a strategy of conditional Nrxns deletion in mice demonstrated that Nrxns regulate neurotransmission through different mechanisms in a cell type-specific manner (Chen et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from previous studies with citations.

claim: Previous work provided evidence for the presence of Nrxn mRNA in mesencephalic DA neurons.
source: Previous work provided evidence for the presence of Nrxn mRNA in mesencephalic DA neurons (Uchigashima et al., 2019; Uchigashima et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement cites previous work showing Nrxn expression in DA neurons.

claim: No study has previously compared the levels of expression of each Nrxn in DA neurons.
source: However, no study has previously compared the levels of expression of each Nrxn in this neuronal population.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: DA neurons are key regulators of movement, motivation, and reward-dependent learning.
source: DA neurons are key regulators of movement, motivation, and reward-dependent learning and several studies using mouse lines with impaired DA transmission reported deficits in basal or psychostimulant-evoked locomotion and learning on the accelerating rotarod (Birgner et al., 2010; Ogura et al., 2005; Zhou and Palmiter, 1995).
evidence: This statement describes DA neuron function with citations.

claim: Mouse lines with impaired DA transmission show deficits in basal or psychostimulant-evoked locomotion and learning on the accelerating rotarod.
source: DA neurons are key regulators of movement, motivation, and reward-dependent learning and several studies using mouse lines with impaired DA transmission reported deficits in basal or psychostimulant-evoked locomotion and learning on the accelerating rotarod (Birgner et al., 2010; Ogura et al., 2005; Zhou and Palmiter, 1995).
evidence: This statement reports findings from previous studies with citations.

claim: Loss of Nrxns in DA neurons leads to some alteration of the functionality of the DA system and some DA-dependent behaviors.
source: The finding of reduced behavioral response to amphetamine suggests that loss of Nrxns in DA neurons leads to some alteration of the functionality of the DA system and some DA-dependent behaviors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amphetamine locomotion data.

claim: Altered DA neurotransmission is often associated with changes in states of hedonia.
source: Because altered DA neurotransmission is often associated with changes in states of hedonia, we next examined the performance of the mice in a well-established sucrose preference task (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This statement provides rationale for the sucrose preference experiment based on general knowledge.

claim: The response of DAT::NrxnsKO mice to natural rewards is unaltered.
source: These findings suggest that the response of DAT::NrxnsKO mice to natural rewards was unaltered.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sucrose preference test data.

claim: The reduced locomotor response to amphetamine in DAT::NrxnsKO mice suggests the possibility that the structure or function of DA neurons or their terminals in the striatum are altered in the absence of Nrxns.
source: The reduced locomotor response to amphetamine in DAT::NrxnsKO mice suggests the possibility that the structure or the function of DA neurons or their terminals in the striatum are altered in the absence of Nrxns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amphetamine locomotion data.

claim: Loss of Nrxns123 does not impair the basic ultrastructure of DA release sites in the vSTR.
source: Together, these results show that loss of Nrxns123 does not impair the basic ultrastructure of DA release sites in the vSTR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy data.

claim: The impaired response to amphetamine suggests a perturbation of extracellular DA dynamics or DA action on target cells.
source: The impaired response to amphetamine suggests a perturbation of extracellular DA dynamics or DA action on target cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amphetamine locomotion data.

claim: Extracellular stimulation recruits striatal cholinergic interneurons that greatly amplify DA axonal release through nicotinic receptor activation.
source: Because extracellular stimulation also recruits striatal cholinergic interneurons that greatly amplify DA axonal release through nicotinic receptor activation (Liu et al., 2022; Rice and Cragg, 2004; Threlfell et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Zhang and Sulzer, 2004), we next isolated direct DA release from cholinergic regulation by blocking nicotinic receptors using dihydro-β-erythroidine hydrobromide (DHβE, 10 µM).
evidence: This statement describes a known mechanism with citations.

claim: Direct DA release isolated by blocking nicotinic receptors is greatly reduced compared to release evoked in normal saline.
source: Direct DA release isolated in this way was greatly reduced compared to release evoked in normal saline (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–L), in line with previous work.
evidence: This observation is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Neurexins regulate activity-dependent DA overflow through both direct and indirect mechanisms.
source: Together these observations suggest that Nrxns regulate activity-dependent DAo through both direct and indirect mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FSCV data.

claim: DA neurons can release GABA or glutamate at a subset of their axon terminals.
source: Because DA neurons can also release GABA or glutamate at a subset of their axon terminals, we also examined whether loss of Nrxns in DA neurons alters GABA or glutamate-mediated synaptic currents evoked by optogenetic activation of DA neuron axons.
evidence: This statement provides background knowledge about DA neuron co-transmission.

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs are blocked by picrotoxin, confirming their GABAergic nature.
source: oIPSCs were blocked by picrotoxin (50 µM), confirming their GABAergic nature (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a pharmacological validation of the recorded currents.

claim: Optically evoked IPSCs are blocked by reserpine, in line with previous work showing that GABA release by DA neurons requires VMAT2.
source: Furthermore, oIPSCs were blocked after superfusion with the VMAT2 inhibitor reserpine (1 µM), in line with previous work showing that GABA release by DA neurons paradoxically requires VMAT2 (Tritsch et al., 2014; Tritsch et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a pharmacological validation consistent with previous literature.

claim: The increase in oIPSC amplitude in the vSTR is likely due to a presynaptic effect.
source: Thus, these results suggest that Nrxns are not influencing GABA receptor dynamics and the increase of oIPSC amplitude is likely due to a presynaptic effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: Neurexins act as regulators of GABA co-transmission by DA neurons in a region-specific manner.
source: These results suggest that Nrxns act as regulators of GABA co-transmission by DA neurons in a region-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data showing differences between vSTR and dSTR.

claim: Neurexins do not have a major role in regulating glutamate release from DA neurons.
source: These results suggest that Nrxns do not have a major role in regulating glutamate release from DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of changes in optically evoked EPSCs.

claim: The region-specific increase of GABA release from DA axons in DAT::NrxnsKO mice could result from different mechanisms.
source: The region-specific increase of GABA release from DA axons in DAT::NrxnsKO mice, identified in our optogenetic experiments, could result from different mechanisms.
evidence: This statement introduces possible mechanisms to explain the findings.

claim: One or more neurexins may act as a repressor of GABA co-transmission and regulate the excitatory/inhibitory neurotransmission balance of the axonal domain of DA neurons.
source: A possible hypothesis to explain our observations is that one or more Nrxns act as a repressor of GABA co-transmission and thus regulate the excitatory/inhibitory neurotransmission balance of the axonal domain of DA neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the findings.

claim: Previous work has shown that neurexins physically and functionally interact with GABAA receptors and that overexpression of neurexins decreases inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic strength.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that Nrxns physically and functionally interact with GABAA receptors and that overexpression of Nrxns decreases inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic strength (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites previous work to support the hypothesis.

claim: After removal of all neurexins, GABA-mediated synaptic currents evoked by stimulation of DA neuron terminals are increased, perhaps in part through altered regulation of GABAA receptors.
source: These results are consistent with our observations showing that after removal of all Nrxns, GABA-mediated synaptic currents evoked by stimulation of DA neuron terminals are increased, perhaps in part through altered regulation of GABAA receptors (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data in the context of previous literature.

claim: The regional specificity of the data raises intriguing questions regarding functional differences between the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal projections.
source: The regional specificity of our data raises intriguing questions regarding functional differences between the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal projections.
evidence: This is a discussion point about the implications of the findings.

claim: There may be intrinsic differences in the structure and function of GABA release sites in the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal circuits.
source: Together, these observations suggest that there may be intrinsic differences in the structure and function of GABA release sites in these two circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regional differences observed in the data.

claim: Neurexins do not appear to act as major regulators of glutamate co-release by DA neurons.
source: Nrxns therefore do not appear to act as major regulators of glutamate co-release by DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of changes in optically evoked EPSCs.

claim: The findings highlight the complexity and diversity of the role of neurexins at synapses.
source: These findings highlight the complexity and the diversity of the role of Nrxns at synapses, in line with much recent work (Chen et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement places the findings in the context of recent literature.

claim: DA regulates tonic inhibition in striatal MSNs, and this regulation differs between D1 and D2 MSNs.
source: Previous work has shown that DA regulates tonic inhibition in striatal MSNs, and this regulation differs between D1 and D2 MSNs (Janssen et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement cites previous work to suggest future directions.

claim: The increase in GABA IPSCs detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice is likely due to an increase in GABA release from DA neurons.
source: Mechanistically, the increase in GABA IPSCs we detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice is likely due to an increase in GABA release from DA neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: Increased GABA uptake by DA neuron terminals and increased GABA vesicular packaging through VMAT2 could lead to increased GABA release.
source: Together these two mechanisms could lead to increased GABA uptake by DA neuron terminals (possibly through GAT1/4) and increased GABA vesicular packaging through a VMAT2-dependent process (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the GABA uptake and VMAT2 data.

claim: The lack of significant increase in VMAT2 in the dSTR could potentially explain why GABA release from DA neuron terminals was not increased in this part of the striatum.
source: The lack of significant increase in VMAT2 in the dSTR could potentially explain why GABA release from DA neuron terminals was not increased in this part of the striatum even though an increase in GABA uptake was detected globally in both VTA and SNc neurons in the in vitro GABA uptake experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation attempting to reconcile different observations.

claim: The increase in oIPSC amplitude in the vSTR was not accompanied by changes in sIPSC amplitude.
source: The increase in oIPSC amplitude in the vSTR was not accompanied by changes in sIPSC amplitude. This further supports the idea that the changes observed in GABA-mediated currents resulted specifically from an increase in presynaptic GABA release from DA neurons (Figure 8).
evidence: This observation supports a presynaptic mechanism, though the sIPSC data is not explicitly shown in the manuscript.

claim: The trend for prolongation of oIPSCs detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice may suggest that deletion of Nrxns from DA terminals increased the expression of postsynaptic GABA receptors.
source: The trend for prolongation of oIPSCs that we detected in DAT::NrxnsKO mice may suggest that deletion of Nrxns from DA terminals increased the expression of postsynaptic GABA receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the trend in decay tau.

claim: A presynaptic mechanism is more likely the primary driver of the increased oIPSC amplitude observed in the vSTR.
source: Thus, it is more likely that a presynaptic mechanism is the primary driver of the increased oIPSC amplitude observed in the vSTR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology data.

claim: Neurexins are dispensable for the initial establishment of axon terminals and synapses by DA neurons but play a role in regulating both the kinetics of DA overflow and GABA release by DA neurons.
source: Together, our findings shed new light on the role of these cell adhesion molecules in DA neuron connectivity. We conclude that Nrxns are dispensable for the initial establishment of axon terminals and synapses by DA neurons but play a role in regulating both the kinetics of DAo and GABA release by DA neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Only a small subset of axon terminals established by DA neurons adopt a synaptic configuration.
source: Only a small subset of axon terminals established by DA neurons adopt a synaptic configuration.
evidence: This statement summarizes a key finding about DA neuron connectivity.

claim: The formation of synaptic contacts by DA neurons must be regulated by other trans-synaptic proteins.
source: We conclude that the formation of such synaptic contacts must be regulated by other trans-synaptic proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that Nrxns are not required for synapse formation.

claim: The findings are globally compatible with a recent study evaluating the impact of deleting neurexins from 5-HT neurons and showing reduced 5-HT release.
source: Our findings are globally compatible with those of a recent study evaluating the impact of deleting Nrxns from 5-HT neurons and showing reduced 5-HT release (Cheung et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement compares the findings to a recent study on another modulatory neuron type.

claim: Most studies on neurexins have been conducted on glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons, with no evaluation of their role in modulatory neurons.
source: Most of these studies have been conducted on glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons, with no evaluation of their role in modulatory neurons such as DA, serotonin, norepinephrine, or acetylcholine neurons, whose connectivity is strikingly different and markedly less synaptic (Ducrot et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: The connectivity of modulatory neurons is strikingly different and markedly less synaptic than glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons.
source: Most of these studies have been conducted on glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons, with no evaluation of their role in modulatory neurons such as DA, serotonin, norepinephrine, or acetylcholine neurons, whose connectivity is strikingly different and markedly less synaptic (Ducrot et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement describes a key difference in connectivity with citation.

claim: The DAT gene is turned on at around embryonic days 14-15.
source: Considering that the DAT gene is turned on at around embryonic days 14–15, the gene deletion is expected to have happened at early stages of the establishment of DA neuron connectivity.
evidence: This statement provides information about the timing of DAT expression.

claim: More extensive changes in the basic connectivity of DA neurons could perhaps have been detected with an earlier knockout.
source: More extensive changes in the basic connectivity of DA neurons could perhaps have been detected with an earlier KO.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Loss of neurexins is associated with impaired DA neurotransmission in the brain of adult mice.
source: We found that loss of Nrxns is associated with impaired DA neurotransmission in the brain of adult mice, as revealed by impaired amphetamine-induced locomotion, altered expression of key DA neuron markers, and a reduced activity-dependent DAo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The axonal ultrastructure of DA neuron terminals is unaltered in DAT::NrxnsKO mice.
source: However, the axonal ultrastructure of DA neuron terminals was unaltered.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the electron microscopy findings.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings reveal an unexpected increase of GABA co-release by DA neurons in the absence of neurexins.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of GABA and glutamate release by DA neuron axons also revealed an unexpected increase of GABA co-release by DA neurons in the absence of Nrxns.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the electrophysiology findings.

claim: Although neurexins may not be required for the basic axonal development of DA neurons, they act as regulators of GABA and DA signaling in these neurons.
source: Together these findings suggest that, although Nrxns may not be required for the basic axonal development of DA neurons, they act as regulators of GABA and DA signaling in these neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Neurexins have been previously suggested to contribute to the development of synapses.
source: Nrxns have been previously suggested to contribute to the development of synapses (Aoto et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Etherton et al., 2009; Li et al., 2007; Missler et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement cites previous work on neurexin function.

claim: The observation of an absence of major structural changes in DA neuron terminals after deletion of neurexins is in keeping with previous reports obtained with single, double, or triple deletion of Nrxn in glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons.
source: Our observation of an absence of major structural changes in the DA neuron terminals after deletion of Nrxns is also in keeping with previous reports obtained with the single, double, or triple deletion of Nrxn in glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons (Chen et al., 2017; Missler et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement compares the findings to previous studies with citations.

claim: A recent study using triple Nrxn mice reported no changes of synapse formation at the calyx of Held.
source: Another recent study using the triple Nrxn mice also reported no changes of synapse formation at the calyx of Held (Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement cites a recent study with similar findings.

claim: Neurexins do not act as necessary drivers of axon terminal and synapse formation by DA neurons.
source: We similarly conclude that Nrxns do not act as necessary drivers of axon terminal and synapse formation by DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy data.

claim: DA neuron terminals in the striatum were identified based on TH immunoreactivity, an approach that may miss some terminals containing low levels of this enzyme.
source: In the present experiments, DA neuron terminals in the striatum were identified based on TH immunoreactivity, an approach that may miss some terminals containing low levels of this enzyme.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a potential limitation of the method.

claim: Glutamate-releasing terminals established by DA neurons can be identified by the presence of VGLUT2.
source: Further immuno-EM experiments would however be required to examine glutamate-releasing terminals established by DA neurons and that can be identified by the presence of VGLUT2 (Bérubé-Carrière et al., 2009; Dal Bo et al., 2004; El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Fortin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement describes a method for identifying glutamate-releasing terminals with citations.

claim: Neurexin123, although not playing an obligatory role in the DA release mechanism and in the initial formation and function of DA neuron varicosities, act as regulators of DA secretion.
source: However, in the presence of a nicotinic receptor antagonist, KO mice showed a clear reduction of peak DAo, suggesting that Nrxn123, although not playing an obligatory role in the DA release mechanism and in the initial formation and function of DA neuron varicosities, act as regulators of DA secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FSCV data in the presence of DHβE.

claim: Slowed kinetics of recovery of extracellular DA in DAT::NrxnsKO mice could result either from reduced DAT function or from prolonged cholinergic amplification of DA neuron terminal activation.
source: This could result either from reduced DAT function or from prolonged cholinergic amplification of DA neuron terminal activation.
evidence: This statement proposes two possible mechanisms to explain the observation.

claim: No significant change in the kinetics of DA overflow recovery was observed when recordings were performed in the presence of DHβE, arguing against reduced DAT function and in favor of prolonged cholinergic amplification.
source: Arguing against the former and in favor of the later, we observed no significant change in the kinetics of DAo recovery when recordings were performed in the presence of the nicotinic antagonist DHßE.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FSCV data in the presence of DHβE.

claim: Neurexins can regulate the localization of terminal nicotinic receptors in hippocampal neurons.
source: Previous work has suggested that Nrxns can regulate the localization of terminal nicotinic receptors in hippocampal neurons (Cheng et al., 2009), but this has never been examined in DA neurons.
evidence: This statement cites previous work and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: The reduced response to amphetamine in DAT::NrxnsKO mice could result from reduced DA stores in DA neuron terminals.
source: This reduced response to amphetamine could perhaps result from reduced DA stores in DA neuron terminals.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the amphetamine locomotion data.

claim: Reduced DA stores in terminals is not consistent with unchanged levels of TH and VMAT2 in the dSTR and increased VMAT2 in the vSTR.
source: However, this is not consistent with our observation of unchanged levels of TH and VMAT2 in the dSTR and increased VMAT2 in the vSTR.
evidence: This statement argues against the hypothesis of reduced DA stores based on the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Amphetamine increases extracellular DA levels by impairing vesicular storage of DA and inducing reverse transport through the DAT.
source: Amphetamine is well known to increase extracellular DA levels by impairing vesicular storage of DA and inducing reverse transport through the DAT.
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of action of amphetamine.

claim: Neurexins may regulate the stability and function of the DAT in DA neuron axon terminals, perhaps through DAT's PDZ domain.
source: It is possible that Nrxns regulate the stability and function of the DAT in DA neuron axon terminals, perhaps through DAT's PDZ domain, and that in the absence of Nrxns, DAT function and positioning in terminals is impaired (Sørensen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism with citation.

claim: Reduced DAT levels in the vSTR of Nrxn KO mice may be implicated in the reduced locomotor response to amphetamine by limiting the extent of DA reverse transport.
source: It is thus possible that reduced DAT levels in the vSTR of Nrxn KO mice is implicated in the reduced locomotor response to amphetamine by limiting the extent of DA reverse transport.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the amphetamine locomotion data.

claim: The increase in VMAT2 immunolabeled surface in the vSTR could reflect a broader distribution of the protein in axonal varicosities and/or an increase in the axonal domain of DA neurons.
source: This could possibly reflect a broader distribution of the protein in axonal varicosities and/or an increase in the axonal domain of DA neurons, similar to a previous observation seen in conditional D2 KO mice (Giguère et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the VMAT2 data with citation.

claim: One possibility is that electrical activation of cholinergic axonal release sites is increased in the DAT:NrxnsKO mice, thus compensating for the reduced primary DA release.
source: One possibility is that electrical activation of cholinergic axonal release sites is increased in the DAT:NrxnsKO mice, thus compensating for the reduced primary DA release.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why reduced peak DA overflow was only detected in the presence of DHβE.

claim: Loss of neurexins from DA terminals may trans-synaptically perturb cholinergic terminals.
source: This could be because loss of Nrxns from DA terminals trans-synaptically perturbs cholinergic terminals, in line with the work mentioned previously and suggesting that Nrxns can regulate the localization of terminal nicotinic receptors in some neurons (Cheng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism with citation.

claim: The origin of the region-specific increase in GABA release is presently unclear but could arise from several possibilities including differential expression of Nrxn splice variants or their postsynaptic ligands and selective binding affinity in the dSTR or vSTR.
source: The origin of this selectivity is presently unclear but could arise from several possibilities including differential expression of Nrxn splice variants or their postsynaptic ligands and selective binding affinity in the dSTR or vSTR.
evidence: This statement proposes possible mechanisms for the regional specificity.

claim: Different Nrxn isoforms have been proposed to regulate various aspects of synapse organization and function.
source: Multiple studies over the past decade reported similar conclusions, where different Nrxn isoforms were proposed to regulate various aspects of synapse organization and function (Ullrich et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement cites previous work on Nrxn isoform function.

claim: Neurexins physically and functionally interact with GABAA receptors.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that Nrxns physically and functionally interact with GABAA receptors and that overexpression of Nrxns decreases inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic strength (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites previous work on Nrxn-GABAA receptor interactions.

claim: Overexpression of neurexins decreases inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic strength.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that Nrxns physically and functionally interact with GABAA receptors and that overexpression of Nrxns decreases inhibitory but not excitatory synaptic strength (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement cites previous work on the effect of Nrxn overexpression.

claim: Baseline GABA uptake is higher in SNc than VTA DA neurons.
source: Furthermore, basal GABA uptake was higher in SNc than VTA DA neurons and baseline oIPSC amplitude was higher in the dSTR than the vSTR.
evidence: This is a summary of the GABA uptake data.

claim: Baseline oIPSC amplitude is higher in the dSTR than the vSTR.
source: Furthermore, basal GABA uptake was higher in SNc than VTA DA neurons and baseline oIPSC amplitude was higher in the dSTR than the vSTR.
evidence: This observation is stated but the data is not explicitly shown in the figures.

claim: There may be intrinsic differences in the structure and function of GABA release sites in the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal circuits.
source: Together, these observations suggest that there may be intrinsic differences in the structure and function of GABA release sites in these two circuits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regional differences in GABA uptake and oIPSC amplitude.

claim: One possible mechanism underlying the increase in GABA release from DA neurons in the DAT::NrxnsKO is increased GABA uptake, leading to increased vesicular packaging and subsequent release.
source: This observation suggests that one possible mechanism underlying the increase in GABA release from DA neurons in the DAT::NrxnsKO is increased GABA uptake, leading to increased vesicular packaging and subsequent release.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the GABA uptake data.

claim: DA neurons do not synthesize GABA using glutamic acid decarboxylase and do not express the vesicular GABA transporter.
source: While DA neurons have the capacity to co-release GABA, it is well established that they do not synthesize it using glutamic acid decarboxylase and do not express the vesicular GABA transporter (Tritsch et al., 2014; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes a known characteristic of DA neurons with citations.

claim: DA neurons use plasma membrane transporters to uptake GABA from the extracellular medium and VMAT2 to package it into synaptic vesicles.
source: Instead, they have been shown to use plasma membrane transporters to uptake GABA from the extracellular medium and VMAT2 to package it into synaptic vesicles (Melani and Tritsch, 2022; Tritsch et al., 2014; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of GABA uptake and packaging in DA neurons with citations.
